## Report on Feynman, *Appendix F: Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle*

**1. The question, frozen.** The title is *Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle*; the opening paragraph names the spread of estimates of "a failure with loss of vehicle and of human life", 1 in 100 to 1 in 100,000, and asks for "the causes and consequences of this lack of agreement". So the central question: **what produces the gap between the working engineers' and management's estimates of Shuttle failure, and what follows from it?** Over the whole programme and its sectors, from certification records and interviews. A forward question — what produces it. (The narrower questions — why 51-L was accepted, whether the SSME was deteriorating — hang off this one.)

**2. The parts.**
A The gap: engineers ≈1/100; Rocketdyne 1/10,000; Marshall 1/300; NASA management 1/100,000.
B The mechanism: a launch schedule engineering cannot keep up with; criteria loosened argument by argument until flights certify in time.
C The rule doing the loosening: "the same risk was flown before without failure" accepted as an argument for safety.
D Why that rule is wrong here: erosion and blow-by are not what the design expected, so they are warnings, not reassurance.
E The "safety factor of three" inversion: with a design that expects no erosion, any erosion is a design failure, not one-third of a margin.
F The erosion model: physical at the gas, empirically fitted at the rubber (.58 power from a nearest line; points twice above and below it).
G Management's low number: a bid for funding, or sincere belief.
H The consequence: ordinary citizens encouraged to fly.
I The generalisation: the SSME certification story is "closely analogous".
J The counter-case: avionics software is checked bottom-up with an independent adversary group; no gradual fooling there.
K A guess: 1/500 per engine per mission, from the solved/unsolved problem list.
L Recommendations.

**3. Change list.** Covered: which equipment (SRB, SSME, avionics sensors, avionics software); length of flight history; erosion depth and blow-by across flights and joints; power level (104% vs 109%); who is estimating; early firm criteria vs later loosened ones; schedule slack vs none. Left out, said up front: the Orbiter and External Tank ("No similar study… were made"); other NASA programmes; where the true rate lies between the two estimates.

**4. Part by part.** Never added up.

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A | held | Quoted from testimony and reports; remove it and there is no question |
| B | held | Remove it, the gap has no producer; it also does the SSME job unchanged |
| C | held | Remove it, the certification stories collapse; the same rule appears in the failed temperature sensors |
| D | held | Held by the design intent, not by opinion: no erosion was designed for |
| E | held | Held by the bridge analogy; remove the inversion and "safety factor of three" stands |
| F | held | Remove it, "understanding vs curve-fitting" loses its worked example |
| G | two routes | Funding or sincerity; either does the job, neither is tested |
| H | borrowed | Rests on the airliner comparison — airline risk is not tested here |
| I | held | Held by the parallel certification records; swap SRB for SSME and it still works |
| J | held | Does the job of narrowing the range; without it the claim is "all of NASA", which this contradicts |
| K | held if | Held only by Feynman's own 13-early/3-late list; that job is his, not the owner's |
| L | fixed | Prescriptions the owner set; not up for test |

**5. Whole-explanation checks.**
*Flip.* Had Challenger flown safely, the gap in the documents would still need explaining. Had the estimates been reversed, B and C could not have covered it — they push one way. It sticks its neck out.
*Direction.* He keeps the physical behaviour (erosion, cracks) apart from the quoted number, and pokes the equipment, not the reports. The number is a reading; the erosion is the thing read.
*Poke.* For B: schedule slack should let the criteria hold; renaming the forms should not matter. For D: a fully bounded erosion process would make acceptance safe; which log recorded the erosion should not matter.
*Answer among the starting points.* "Management exaggerates reliability… to the point of fantasy" sits close to the conclusion, and the closing "public relations" line reaches back to it. The sincere-belief alternative keeps it from a closed circle, but the motive itself carries no separate evidence.
*Add a job.* What should happen where schedule pressure meets a check that can fail? The software case. That job genuinely shrinks the range from "NASA" to "where the check cannot catch you".
*Pull.* G's two motives fight; the same flights used as evidence of safety are the flights that produced erosion — Feynman names that join, his tightest move; and "top-down is bad" fights the admitted high quality of SSME work. He draws that line at expensive-to-fix, and names what would show it misplaced (a cheap top-down fix).
*Catch-all.* "Engineering judgment" is NASA's own bin, inserted in place of a number. Feynman asks it for a gauge and it cannot give one — the two judgments disagree by a thousandfold.
*Rival.* "The low number is right; 51-L was an outlier." Told apart by the physical record: cracks as early as 1,150 seconds, erosion varying flight to flight. Checked, not assumed.
*Provenance.* A, B, C, F seen — testimony, the JPL study, the records. D, E built. E borrows ordinary engineering practice. G asserted ("One reason may be… The other may be…"). K built on a fitted pattern.

**6. What would make it harder to vary.** Put the engineers' figures to management in writing and record what happened to them — did the low number go into funding requests, or did the high number go in and get overridden? One document turns G from two routes into held or idle. Second: write K's falsifier down first — what size of failure in the next 250,000 seconds would show the guess wrong.

**7. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. That the criteria slipped does not fix the true probability; Feynman says as much ("difficult to be more accurate"), and K is a guess.

**8. One next step.** Run the same test on a case where criteria were *tightened* under schedule pressure. If the mechanism only ever runs one way, find what makes it one-way.

That's a forward/production question: what produces the disagreement (and, downstream, the loss of the vehicle). - Part A: Management's estimate is ~1/100,000 (from the document, claims).

- Part C: The mechanism — certification criteria gradually decreasing strictness ("gradually decreasing strictness", waivers, accepting the same risk flown before as evidence of safety).

- Part I: Consequences — ordinary citizens encouraged to fly, McAuliffe.
